Two Flavors of Growth based Accountability

These two approaches to growth impart different levels of stringency

Norm-referenced Is the group of students growing better/worse (on
average) than statistical expectation?
Criterion-referenced Is each student in the group growing at a sufficient
rate to reach/maintain proficient status?

The first judges against statistical expectation,
The second judges against a common, desirable destination we
want all students to reach (at a minimum).

Norm-referenced student growth/accountability

Using student growth percentiles, the median SGP for a group
describes whether students in the group, on “average”,
demonstrated growth above or below expectation.
This is essentially, what value-added models quantify.
Value-added models go an extra step an implicitly infer causality by
labeling the aggregate measure as a school or teacher effect.
Some value-added models include student level characteristics
(e.g., demographics) and thus set differential expectations.
Student growth percentiles do not include student level
characteristics in the model. Any adjustments needed for
accountability purposes can occur post-hoc.

Criterion-referenced student growth/accountability

Former Secretary of Education Margaret Spellings initiated the
growth model pilot program allowing states to include growth as a
means of satisfying AYP.
The “Bright Line Principle” of all students being proficient by 2014
remained.
15 states were accepted as part of the pilot. None saw a significant
improvement in their AYP numbers.
An impossible goal should be impossible regardless of how you
“slice it” (via status or growth).
Colorado successfully applied to be a part of the growth model pilot
program using student growth percentiles/percentile growth
trajectories.

Combining Norm- and Criterion-referenced growth
We feel that value-added models and growth-to-standard models fail
in isolation because each ignores the other.
In all pursuits, we need both norms and criteria to make sense of the
world.
Student growth percentiles/percentile growth trajectories provide the
basis for combining a norm- and criterion-referenced view of growth.

Student Growth Percentiles describe what is. A median SGP
describes what is on “average”.
Percentile growth trajectories (target SGPs) describe what should be.
A median target SGP describes what should be on “average.
Comparing the median SGP to the median target SGP allows one to
have both a norm- and criterion-referenced interpretation of growth.
Colorado developed its school performance framework around this
idea. New York is actively exploring this idea for AYP.
